problem.title: Fixing CompletableFuture commonPool() Starvation & Nested Join Deadlocks

spark.summary: Diagnose and remediate a Java microservice suffering 504 Gateway Timeouts caused by blocking HTTP/DB I/O and nested .join() calls on ForkJoinPool.commonPool().
spark.keyTakeaway: Isolate I/O onto a bounded Executor or Virtual Threads, replace nested .join() with thenComposeAsync(), and add orTimeout() + ArchUnit guardrails to restore sub-20ms P99 latency.
spark.byteSummary:
A Java microservice running on 4-vCPU Kubernetes pods begins hanging with 504 Gateway Timeouts under moderate traffic, even though CPU utilization is near 0%. Thread dumps reveal all 3 `ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-*` threads parked in `CompletableFuture.waitingGet` (from nested `.join()` calls) while hundreds of subtasks sit in the submission queue.

Because every `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync()` call omitted an `Executor` argument, blocking JDBC and HTTP calls shared the tiny 3-thread `commonPool()`, causing self-deadlock whenever concurrent requests triggered nested futures.

Remediation isolates blocking I/O onto a dedicated bounded `ExecutorService` (or Java 21 Virtual Threads with `Semaphore` caps), refactors nested `.join()` into non-blocking `thenComposeAsync()`, adds `orTimeout()` + `.exceptionally()` per fan-out branch, and adds ArchUnit CI checks to restore sub-20ms P99.

learningJourney.title: Stage 1: Thread-Dump Triage — Zero CPU & 504 Timeouts
learningJourney.purpose: Recognize the thread-dump signature of ForkJoinPool.commonPool() starvation when CPU is idle.
learningJourney.explanation: When a service hits 504 timeouts at < 5% CPU, inspect `jcmd <pid> Thread.print`. Seeing all `ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-*` threads in `WAITING` at `CompletableFuture.waitingGet` (or `TIMED_WAITING` on socket reads) alongside a growing `getQueuedSubmissionCount()` confirms `commonPool()` starvation.

sectionDiagram.title: Spotting commonPool() Deadlock in Thread Dumps & Pod Metrics

nodes.label: 504 Timeouts @ 3% CPU
nodes.sub: Pod looks idle on CPU graph

cards.label: Deceptive CPU Metrics
cards.detail: Blocked I/O threads consume 0% CPU, making autoscalers fail to scale out during a pool deadlock.

cards.label: Container Math
cards.detail: On a 4-vCPU pod, commonPool() only has 3 threads—3 concurrent requests can lock the entire pod.

sectionDiagram.summary: Low CPU paired with 504s and commonPool workers parked in waitingGet points directly to commonPool() starvation.
sectionDiagram.caption: 504 timeouts at low CPU with commonPool workers parked in waitingGet identify nested .join() starvation.

learningJourney.title: Stage 2: Auditing Implicit commonPool() Call Sites
learningJourney.purpose: Locate every hidden CompletablFuture method that silently falls back to ForkJoinPool.commonPool().
learningJourney.explanation: It is not enough to fix `supplyAsync(fn)`: `thenApplyAsync(fn)`, `thenComposeAsync(fn)`, `runAsync(fn)`, and `handleAsync(fn)` ALL default to `commonPool()` if the `Executor` parameter is omitted. Auditing both initial submissions and downstream `*Async` continuations ensures no stage leaks back onto `commonPool()`.

sectionDiagram.title: Eliminating Every Implicit commonPool() Fallback in Async Chains

cards.label: Sync vs *Async
cards.detail: Non-Async methods (thenApply) run on the completing thread; *Async methods without an Executor jump to commonPool().

cards.label: Third-Party Libraries
cards.detail: Verify SDKs and HTTP clients are configured with their own event loops or thread pools.

sectionDiagram.summary: Both initial supplyAsync() calls and downstream *Async() continuations fall back to commonPool() unless an Executor is passed.
sectionDiagram.caption: Every 1-arg *Async() method and parallelStream() call must be audited to pass explicit isolated Executors.

learningJourney.title: Stage 3: Refactoring Nested .join() into thenComposeAsync()
learningJourney.purpose: Convert blocking parent-child future calls into a flat, non-blocking asynchronous pipeline.
learningJourney.explanation: Refactor the outer `supplyAsync(() -> { var x = inner.join(); ... })` anti-pattern into `fetchOuterAsync(ioPool).thenComposeAsync(outer -> fetchInnerAsync(outer, ioPool), ioPool)`. Because no thread ever parks waiting on a child future, even a small bounded pool handles deep dependency graphs without self-deadlocking.

sectionDiagram.title: Flattening Nested .join() into Non-Blocking thenComposeAsync()

cards.label: Zero Parked Threads
cards.detail: Between Step 1 and Step 2, zero threads are blocked waiting in waitingGet.

cards.label: Exception Propagation
cards.detail: Failures in Step 1 skip Step 2 automatically and flow to .exceptionally() or .handle().

sectionDiagram.summary: Flattening nested .join() calls into thenComposeAsync() eliminates parent-child thread dependency deadlocks.
sectionDiagram.caption: Flat thenComposeAsync() pipelines release threads between I/O steps and enforce 200 ms orTimeout() deadlines.

learningJourney.title: Stage 4: Bounded I/O Pool Sizing & Backpressure
learningJourney.purpose: Configure dedicated I/O ThreadPoolExecutors with bounded queues and rejection policies to avoid OOMs.
learningJourney.explanation: For platform-thread I/O pools, size `corePoolSize`/`maxPoolSize` using Little's Law (`concurrency = QPS * avg_latency_sec`) with a bounded `ArrayBlockingQueue` (e.g., 256-512) and `AbortPolicy` that returns HTTP 429/503 quickly rather than queuing tens of thousands of stale requests into an OOM.

sectionDiagram.title: Little's Law Sizing & Bounded Queue Load Shedding

cards.label: Fail Fast > Queue Forever
cards.detail: Rejecting excess requests in 1 ms with 503 protects healthy in-flight requests and prevents cascading timeouts.

cards.label: Graceful Shutdown
cards.detail: Register shutdown hooks calling executor.shutdown() + awaitTermination() during pod SIGTERM.

sectionDiagram.summary: Sizing I/O pools with Little's Law and bounding queues with AbortPolicy prevents OOMs and cascading latency spikes.
sectionDiagram.caption: Little's Law thread sizing, bounded ArrayBlockingQueue, and AbortPolicy 503 shedding protect service stability.

learningJourney.title: Stage 5: Migrating I/O Pools to Java 21+ Virtual Threads
learningJourney.purpose: Adopt Virtual Threads safely with Semaphore concurrency limits and non-pinning locks.
learningJourney.explanation: Replacing a fixed I/O `ThreadPoolExecutor` with `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` removes platform-thread limits on concurrent I/O. However, unlimited virtual threads can overwhelm downstream DB connection pools—so wrap downstream calls in a `Semaphore` (e.g., 100 permits) and use `ReentrantLock` instead of `synchronized`.

sectionDiagram.title: Virtual Threads + Semaphore Backpressure for Downstream Protection

cards.label: HikariCP Alignment
cards.detail: Match Semaphore permits to downstream connection pool size so virtual threads don't pile up on pool.getConnection().

cards.label: JDK 24+ JEP 491 Note
cards.detail: JDK 24 resolves synchronized pinning, but ReentrantLock remains essential on Java 21 LTS.

sectionDiagram.summary: Virtual threads scale I/O concurrency effortlessly when paired with Semaphore limits and ReentrantLock.
sectionDiagram.caption: VirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor, Semaphore(100), and ReentrantLock scale blocking I/O without carrier pinning or DB overload.

learningJourney.title: Stage 6: Sub-20ms P99 Fan-Out with Timeouts & Cancellation
learningJourney.purpose: Prevent leaked background work when an HTTP request or parent CompletableFuture times out.
learningJourney.explanation: In Java, `CompletableFuture.orTimeout()` completes the future exceptionally, but it does NOT automatically interrupt an underlying blocking HTTP or JDBC call. Pair `orTimeout(20, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)` with client-level socket timeouts (`HttpRequest.timeout()`) and `whenComplete` cancellation hooks so timed-out branches release sockets immediately.

sectionDiagram.title: Aligning CompletableFuture Deadlines with Client Socket Timeouts

cards.label: Zombie Socket Prevention
cards.detail: Always set socket/statement timeouts <= CompletableFuture timeout so timed-out tasks don't leak threads.

cards.label: completeOnTimeout
cards.detail: Prefer completeOnTimeout() over throwing when stale-cache or empty-list fallbacks are acceptable.

sectionDiagram.summary: Matching CompletableFuture deadlines with underlying socket/DB timeouts prevents leaked background I/O and keeps P99 < 20 ms.
sectionDiagram.caption: completeOnTimeout(18 ms) paired with matching HTTP/JDBC socket timeouts protects sub-20ms P99 latency.

learningJourney.title: Stage 7: CI Guardrails & Production Pool Telemetry
learningJourney.purpose: Lock in the fix permanently with ArchUnit static checks, BlockHound tests, and Grafana pool alerts.
learningJourney.explanation: Add an ArchUnit test that fails the build if any service class calls `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync`, `runAsync`, or `*Async` without an `Executor` argument. Run BlockHound in integration tests to catch blocking calls on `ForkJoinPool` threads, and alert if `executor.queue.remainingCapacity` drops below 20%.

sectionDiagram.title: ArchUnit + BlockHound + Micrometer Queue Alerting

cards.label: Preventing Silent Regressions
cards.detail: A single developer adding .thenApplyAsync(fn) without an Executor is caught immediately at compile/test time.

cards.label: Rejections Counter
cards.detail: Alert on any non-zero ThreadPoolExecutor rejected tasks metric to spot capacity exhaustion early.

sectionDiagram.summary: ArchUnit static rules, BlockHound integration tests, and Micrometer queue alerts prevent future commonPool() deadlocks.
sectionDiagram.caption: ArchUnit CI checks, BlockHound profiling, and Micrometer queue alerts guard against commonPool() regressions.

knowledgeChecks.question: What thread-dump signature confirms a `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` deadlock when a Java pod returns 504s at 3% CPU?

options.text: All `ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-*` threads parked in `WAITING` at `CompletableFuture.waitingGet` while `queuedSubmissions > 0`.
options.feedback: Correct. Every worker is blocked in .join()/.get() while queued subtasks wait for a free worker.

options.text: GC threads using 100% of all CPU cores.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Here CPU utilization is near 0%.

options.text: Virtual threads running on 1,000 carrier threads.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Virtual threads unmount during blocking I/O and don't park commonPool() workers.

options.text: HTTP threads throwing `OutOfMemoryError` immediately on startup.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Deadlocked worker threads hang requests until 504 timeouts.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: All commonPool() workers parked in CompletableFuture.waitingGet with non-zero queued submissions is the classic self-deadlock signature.

knowledgeChecks.question: You fixed `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(fn, ioPool)`, but `commonPool()` still gets I/O work. What is the most likely culprit?

options.feedback: Incorrect. orTimeout() uses an internal ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor delayer, not commonPool().

options.text: Calling `.thenComposeAsync(fn)` or `.thenApplyAsync(fn)` later in the chain without passing `ioPool`.
options.feedback: Correct. Every *Async() method without an explicit Executor falls back to ForkJoinPool.commonPool().
Incorrect. Queue type affects backpressure, not which pool *Async() selects.
Incorrect. ReentrantLock prevents virtual thread pinning; it does not route to commonPool().

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Any *Async() continuation without an explicit Executor argument silently switches execution back to ForkJoinPool.commonPool().

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should `CompletableFuture.orTimeout()` be paired with an HTTP/JDBC client socket timeout?

options.text: Because `orTimeout()` only completes the future exceptionally without interrupting the underlying blocking socket/DB thread.
options.feedback: Correct. Without a matching client socket timeout, the hung background thread stays blocked until the OS TCP timeout.
Incorrect. orTimeout() does not affect GC.

options.text: Because `orTimeout()` automatically retries failed SQL queries.
options.feedback: Incorrect. orTimeout() fails the future with TimeoutException; it does not retry.
Incorrect. orTimeout() uses a lightweight delayer thread.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: orTimeout() does not cancel/interrupt blocking I/O on the worker thread, so client socket timeouts are needed to free resources.

beginner.summary: Fix Java microservice hangs by moving blocking I/O off `commonPool()` onto a dedicated pool, chaining with `thenComposeAsync()`, and adding timeouts.
beginner.keyTakeaway: Dedicated I/O pools and non-blocking chaining stop thread starvation and 504 timeouts.
beginner.byteSummary:
If a Java service hangs with 504 errors while CPU is idle, check whether `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync()` is missing a custom thread pool.

Moving blocking calls to a dedicated I/O pool and chaining with `thenComposeAsync()` + `orTimeout()` keeps requests flowing.

intermediate.summary: Audit all 1-arg `*Async()` calls, flatten nested `.join()` into `thenComposeAsync(..., ioPool)`, and size bounded I/O pools via Little's Law.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: Passing explicit `ioPool` to every `*Async()` stage and bounding queues with `AbortPolicy` eliminates self-deadlocks and OOMs.
intermediate.byteSummary: Remediating `commonPool()` deadlocks requires fixing both `supplyAsync()` and downstream `*Async()` continuations, refactoring nested `.join()` into `thenComposeAsync()`, and sizing bounded `ArrayBlockingQueue` I/O pools via Little's Law.

advanced.summary: Adopt Java 21+ Virtual Threads with `Semaphore` caps and `ReentrantLock`, align `completeOnTimeout()` with socket timeouts, and enforce ArchUnit + BlockHound CI gates.
advanced.keyTakeaway: Matching future deadlines to socket timeouts prevents leaked threads, while ArchUnit bans on 1-arg `*Async()` prevent regressions.
advanced.byteSummary:
At scale, `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` paired with `Semaphore` downstream caps and `ReentrantLock` eliminates thread starvation without carrier pinning.

Align `completeOnTimeout()` with HTTP/JDBC socket timeouts, enforce ArchUnit bans on 1-arg `CompletableFuture.*Async()`, and alert on `commonPool()` queue depth.

_nextProblem.prompt: Standard Transformer self-attention computes S = QK^T / sqrt(d), P = softmax(S), and O = PV. At sequence length N = 32,768 with 32 attention heads in FP16, materializing S and P in GPU HBM requires 32 * 32,768^2 * 2 bytes = 68.7 GB per layer—exceeding an 80 GB NVIDIA H100/A100 GPU and saturating HBM memory bandwidth. Design and implement an exact, IO-aware tiled attention algorithm in Python/PyTorch (reference kernel logic) that reduces HBM memory from O(N^2) to O(N) while remaining mathematically identical to standard attention.
